TRANSCRIPT OF PROCEEDINGS
THE HON CATHERINE HOLMES AC SC, Commissioner
THE ROYAL COMMISSION INTO THE ROBODEBT SCHEME
FRIDAY, 9 DECEMBER 2022 AT 9.32 AM (AEST)
DAY 17
MR JUSTIN GREGGERY KC, Senior Counsel Assisting
MR ANGUS SCOTT KC, Senior Counsel Assisting
MR D. FREEBURN, Counsel Assisting
MS DOMINIQUE HOGAN-DORAN SC, for the Commonwealth
MR M. PRUSCINO, for the Commonwealth
MR A. VIAL, for the Commonwealth

COMMISSIONER: Yes. I will just take the day's appearances.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. If it pleases the Commission, I appear with Mr Freeburn again.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you. And Ms Hogan-Doran?
MS HOGAN-DORAN: May it please the Commission, I appear this morning with Mr Pruscino
and this afternoon with Mr Vial.
COMMISSIONER: Alright. Thank you. Yes, Mr Greggery.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. So, Commissioner, Ms Halbert resumes her evidence from yesterday
and is present. I ask that Exhibit 2904 be produced on the screen, please. While that's
happening, Ms Halbert, it is the communication from you to various persons in DSS and
Ms Golightly about the comments on the Exposure Draft - sorry, not the Exposure Draft, the
draft Executive Minute.
MS HALBERT: Mr Greggery, I think - I think this email is to Melissa Ryan, is it?
MR GREGGERY: Melissa Ryan, yes. Can I just clarify with you, though, that this reflected, that
is, the attachment we will come to shortly, the state of mind in respect to the DHS proposal
at that time?
MS HALBERT: Correct.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. And if we could then go to Attachment 2095. That understanding
included, in the second dot point on this page, in respect of the proposal, that in some cases,
there are fundamental impacts on social security policy and law. Do you see that?
MS HALBERT: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And if we go over to page 0193, you will see particularly the comments
which were inserted in the box below. And over to the top of page 0194, these comments
include - sorry, this was the proposal which reflected a fundamental change to the social
security law?
MS HALBERT: That's right.
MR GREGGERY: If we return then to page 0193, you can see under the heading PAYG Clean
Up in subparagraph (b), the last sentence of the proposal indicates that:
The customer will have an opportunity to update the information prior to it being applied to
their Centrelink record.
You can see that?

MR GREGGERY: Perhaps if subparagraph (b) could be called out -
MS HALBERT: Yes, yes.
MR GREGGERY: The ATO information referred to in this paragraph is, of course, the PAYG
summary provided by employers to the ATO?
MS HALBERT: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: Alright. And your understanding of the proposal and the context in which the
DSS position was arrived at included (1) the concept of a smoothing methodology; and (2)
the opportunity to update the information by a customer?
MS HALBERT: That's right.
MR GREGGERY: Prior to the smoothing or averaging -
MS HALBERT: That was our understanding.
MR GREGGERY: - or apportionment leading to the calculation of a debt. Alright. And although
that was the DSS position as at Tuesday, 20 January 2015, and despite some watering down
or softening of language later in the week, that position didn't change in any substantive way
to your state of mind?
MS HALBERT: No. And I wouldn't call it softening of language; we were just refining points
that we were making to DHS, trying to get heard, I guess.
MR GREGGERY: And - that is, the proposal with those characteristics was one known to DSS
at the time that it considered it involved a fundamental change to the law?
MS HALBERT: That's right.
MR GREGGERY: And that position didn't change that week?
MS HALBERT: Not to my knowledge, no.
MR GREGGERY: Alright. And your final communication to Ms Golightly about it was the
Friday, the 26th?
MS HALBERT: Yes. I think it was Friday the 23rd.
MR GREGGERY: 23rd. You're quite right, yes. If I could have Exhibit 2101 produced,
DSS.5023.0001.1305. We have moved from January to February here. And, again, this is just
for context. On Thursday, 26 February, Ms Halbert, you were copied into an email which
attached a revised new draft Brief to Minister Morrison and the communication that

Minister Morrison had indicated that he wanted a number of potential proposals and the
attached Briefing to be brought forward in his Portfolio Budget Submission?
MS HALBERT: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And Mr Kimber had reiterated at that point in the fourth line, if that could be
called out, commencing "PAYG Clean Up", that:
There were potential legal issues with this, and we need to tease these out more specifically
over the coming days.
Do you see that?
MS HALBERT: Yes, I do.
MR GREGGERY: And that Mr Kimber's email in the first dot point below, according to his
understanding of the process, was that DHS were going to draft descriptive words around
the proposals. Although there appears to be a question in the middle of that point:
Is that possible in the timeframe?
And his position that he had reiterated that:
The PAYG Clean Up Proposal needs to have appropriate words re potential legal
risks/retrospectivity.
And that, again, reflected the DSS position at that time?
MS HALBERT: That's right.
MR GREGGERY: If I could ask that Exhibit 2103, DSS.5023.0002.2176, be placed on the
screen. Ms Halbert, you can see in the bottom part of that page that on Wednesday, 4 March
2015, you received the DHS NPPs for inclusion in the 2015/2016 Portfolio Budget
Submission?
MS HALBERT: Yes. And I think I mentioned in my Statement that I had seen that at one
point - and there was one that I might have missed, and this might have been the one. But I
think I was copied in for information - excuse me - but there were small - I'm no longer in the
Dep Sec role.
MR GREGGERY: That's right.
MS HALBERT: And there's small parts of this combined package that pertain to my
substantive job.
MR GREGGERY: That's right. And as you indicate in your Statement, you cannot recall

MS HALBERT: I might well have, but I just don't recall.
MR GREGGERY: And you don't have any recollection of reading it?
MS HALBERT: I don't have any recollection, and I would have read the bits that pertained to
me, of course, but I may not have read that.
MR GREGGERY: I ask that Exhibit 2146_R - sorry, 2146, that is, DSS.5023.0002.2195_R - this
is the attachment, Ms Halbert. Thank you. And if we go to page 2196, underneath the last
redacted passage commencing, "DHS.” Thank you. If you had read the attachment,
Ms Halbert, this is what you would have read?
MS HALBERT: Yes. Presumably.
MR GREGGERY: And no doubt you've read this in the course of preparing for your evidence.
Would you agree with me that the attachment as it was described as the DHS New Policy
Proposal reflected, in the same basic terms, the proposal that was considered by you in the
week of 19 - 20 through to 23 January?
MS HALBERT: At a high level, yes.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. And, particularly, it identified that customers would be required to
confirm information that DHS held about them, that the targeting of historic overpayments
due to income - incorrect income declarations would deliver unspecified amounts in debt
and savings, that it would be based on analysis of PAYG data and transfer the obligation to
the customer. And if we go over the page to 2197. Thank you. And just call out the top
paragraph before the first redactions. Thank you. That is, that it put the obligation on the
customer to ensure their record is correct?
MS HALBERT: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: It went on to insert that:
The new approach would not change how income is assessed or overpayments were
calculated.
But from that point on, what you understood to be the proposal and the number of
interventions, or the number of customers targeted was exactly the same as what had been
addressed in the January advice?
MS HALBERT: I think I would not have such direct knowledge, but on the face of it, yes. Yes.
MR GREGGERY: Despite the sentence there that the new approach will not change how
income is assessed or overpayments are calculated, in your preparation for your evidence
here, on reading that document, you don't see that there's any material difference in the

concepts of retrospectivity or income smoothing in terms of the process that was proposed
and considered in January by yourself and others?
MS HALBERT: On what I'm reading here, I can't tell.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. There doesn't appear to be any change in the substance of the proposal
despite the words in the first dot point there about the process not changing?
MS HALBERT: On the surface of it, it is largely the same proposal.
MR GREGGERY: Largely the same proposal, yes. If we move forward, then, to January 2017.
You became involved in the Ombudsman's investigation?
MS HALBERT: That's right. I was Acting Deputy Secretary at the time. But just before
Christmas that - in 2016, I think, I took on the responsibility for this debt and compliance
function - policy function.
MR GREGGERY: Because of the way in which the allocation of responsibility was redivided?
MS HALBERT: It was a restructure, basically, yes.
MR GREGGERY: A restructure within DSS?
MS HALBERT: That's right.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. And so you came into that role in December 2016?
MS HALBERT: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And at that point, there was very significant media attention in respect of -
MS HALBERT: I believe it was starting.
MR GREGGERY: Starting. It certainly gathered full steam by January -
MS HALBERT: Correct.
MR GREGGERY: - following the Christmas break.
MS HALBERT: That's right.
MR GREGGERY: And in that context, with that additional responsibility, you became involved
in the Ombudsman's investigation?
MS HALBERT: That's right.

MR GREGGERY: I would ask that Exhibit 2104, DSS.5023.0002.2174_R, be placed on the
screen. Thank you. When you became aware of the Ombudsman's investigation, there was
effectively an internal informal investigation to go back and figure out what had happened
which allowed the proposal, as it was considered in January 2015, to be implemented as a
Budget Measure and rolled out as predicted under the New Policy Proposal?
MS HALBERT: Broadly, that's what - we were just trying to work out what had happened.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. And one of the pieces of information that was prepared in the process
of trying to work out what happened was that Ms McGuirk appears to have contacted Mr
Kimber and asked him what his recollections were, and he put them in this email?
MS HALBERT: That's right. We just didn't have many - the staff on hand to - who had a
memory of this.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. And what Mr Kimber put into this email, which was copied to
Ms McGuirk and yourself, together with Ms Wilson and Mr McBride, was the background
and a particular meeting on 27 February to his recollection?
MS HALBERT: That's right.
MR GREGGERY: If the background and the content of the 27 February meeting could be
called out, please. Thank you. The background there, Ms Halbert, reflects what at least you
probably recalled at that time about the DSS position in respect of the proposal as it related
to income smoothing and retrospectivity?
MS HALBERT: I'm not sure I understand what the question was, sorry.
MR GREGGERY: Well, as Mr Kimber describes the background -
MS HALBERT: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: - DSS had provided commentary to DHS in January and February '15 that the
proposed method to use annual income to calculate and raise a debt was not likely to
withstand scrutiny, and if it was to be used, then legislative changes would have to be made.
He goes on to explain why. But at least insofar as he describes that, I'm suggesting that was
consistent with your memory of the DSS commentary to DHS during that period in time.
MS HALBERT: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. The 27 February meeting that he's described - and I don't think you
attended that meeting, did you?
MS HALBERT: No, I don't believe so.
MR GREGGERY: Involves Mr Kimber and Mr McBride and, of course, two persons from DHS,

the new approach would use newly available data sources and analytical tools such that it
would not change how income is assessed or overpayments were calculated. Putting to one
side the fact that that didn't explain what was going to happen rather than what was not
going to happen, it continued that it had the following components:
DHS would target identified discrepancies based on PAYG files obtained from the ATO
compared with reported earnings data that DHS held.
Stopping there, in respect of that dot point, that resembled the proposal that was
considered by DSS in that week in January 2015?
MS HALBERT: I understand that was simply identifying a discrepancy, not raising a debt or
anything.
MR GREGGERY: Certainly. The second dot point is:
Where a significant discrepancy is detected, the information would be presented to the
recipient.
Pause there. At least that had similarity to the proposal considered by DHS in January 2015?
MS HALBERT: I believe so. There may be nuances in it, but I believe so.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. Well, really I'm drawing on the point that the information would be
presented to the customer?
MS HALBERT: That's correct. I mean, that's important, yes.
MR GREGGERY: And the customer would be given the opportunity to comment?
MS HALBERT: That's right. So information hasn't yet been used for customers -
MR GREGGERY: Customers given the opportunity to respond as it was set out in the
document I took you to first?
MS HALBERT: That's right.
MR GREGGERY:
This would not be a debt notice, but rather a recipient would be afforded the opportunity to
explain, correct, update or challenge the information.
Again, that mirrored the opportunity as it was described in the notice?
MS HALBERT: Without trying to be difficult, I - at that point, if we're talking about 2015, I
probably didn't have that level of detail around exact steps. The meeting that I attended in

that - this was an important point, that the ATO information not be used to raise a debt. But I
probably didn't have that level of detail around what opportunities the customer would be
provided with, etcetera, in 2015. I came to learn about that in more detail in 2017.
MR GREGGERY: Well, I suggest that you did have that level of detail in 2015 because it clearly
said so in -
MS HALBERT: Look, as I say, I'm not trying to say I didn't. I'm just saying if there's nuance
under that, I - it was important that the customer have the opportunity to provide further
information. I recall that from 2015.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. That's right. But the opportunity, which is described there, that is, the
presentation of information to a recipient, them being afforded the opportunity to explain,
correct, update or challenge the information, was in broad terms no different to the proposal
that was considered in the week of 25 -
MS HALBERT: That's probably right, yes.
MR GREGGERY: - January 2015, where it said:
The customer -
MS HALBERT: Sorry?
MR GREGGERY: Thank you. Where it said:
The customer will have the opportunity to update the information prior to it being applied to
their Centrelink record.
MS HALBERT: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. The third dot point, as Mr Kimber recalled the meeting, was that:
Any subsequent debt raised would take into account the information provided by the
recipient.
MS HALBERT: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: Again, that was no different to the proposal considered in -
MS HALBERT: That was an element of the original, yes.
MR GREGGERY: It was a part of the original, yes. And:
DHS also advised that there would be no change to how income is assessed, or overpayments
were calculated as part of the proposal.

And if I pause there, you will recall I just took to you the NPP which was copied to you on 4
March 2015 which used those same words but which you considered didn't change the
substance of the use of income smoothing or of the retrospective application.
MS HALBERT: Well, I think DHS was saying that there would be no change from previous
practice in terms of how income is assessed, or overpayments calculated. So despite this
proposal, they - and this is my interpretation of this email, not - I wasn't there. They were
saying, "Despite this proposal, we haven't changed the way we calculate debts and raise
overpayments.” So -
MR GREGGERY: Right. Okay. I might just clarify what your understanding of that meant in a
practical sense. Did you understand that representation, "No change to how income is
assessed, or overpayments were calculated," to be, "We are not going to change in a
fundamental way the use - the way which we calculate debts by income smoothing," or,
alternatively, is it your understanding that income smoothing was always used to calculate
debts and that meant there was no change?
MS HALBERT: I don't think I had that level - I don't think I was familiar with what DHS was
doing in regards to all debts before I got the function in 2017. But I - on my reading of it, I
would say that they are saying, "Despite this proposal, we will continue to assess income and
overpayments on the same basis we had previously," whatever that was.
MR GREGGERY: Whatever that was. And there are two options: one is that income
smoothing was always used to calculate debts about which you had given advice; or that
there was a misrepresentation and income smoothing was now being used -
MS HALBERT: I -
MR GREGGERY: - that hadn't occurred previously?
MS HALBERT: Well, look, I wasn't there at - in this discussion, but I don't believe we as a
Department knew about the income smoothing being used on a broader basis.
MR GREGGERY: That is, on a broader basis prior to the proposal?
MS HALBERT: Prior to this proposal.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. That is, prior to 2015, you were not aware of income smoothing being -
MS HALBERT: No. So we would have assumed that the normal method, whatever that was,
was being used to raise debts and would continue to be used.
MR GREGGERY: That is, a method which did not involve income smoothing?
MS HALBERT: Not involving income smoothing to raise the debt. Correct.

MS HALBERT: Income smoothing would be a source of information - not income smoothing,
the ATO data would be a source of information.
MR GREGGERY: That is, a trigger for a manual investigation?
MS HALBERT: An investigation of some description.
MR GREGGERY: Right. Okay. And so building on that, then, your understanding of what was
represented to Mr Kimber and recorded by him was that ATO data was, under the proposal,
to be used as a trigger for an investigation?
MS HALBERT: That's my understanding.
MR GREGGERY: Right. That is, that that part of the proposal which indicated that income
smoothing would effectively be the default position was not part of the final measure as
implemented?
MS HALBERT: And that was critical, as far as I understand.
MR GREGGERY: It was critical, yes. If we could go, then, down to the next paragraph
commencing, "Subsequent to that meeting," and call that out. Thank you. Mr Kimber refers
to the email on 4 March, to which I took you to, which included the reference to:
DHS advising the new approach would not change the way debts are calculated.
And you have given evidence of your understanding, at least in 2017, about what that
meant. But you don't recall reading the NPP in 2015?
MS HALBERT: I just - I don't recall, but that's not to say I didn't. But I - in 2017, I had this
understanding.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. Alright. If we go back to Exhibit 2107, DSS.5023.0002.2172_R. You can
see that one of the emails that Ms McGuirk obtained as part of looking back to figure out
what had happened was the policy advice from Mr Mason to Mr Whitecross and Mr Joyce in
an email, Friday, 16 January 2015. Do you recall being provided with a copy of that document
in January 2017?
MS HALBERT: I'm not sure if I saw this email, but I believe I saw the advice - well, at some
point saw the advice from David Mason. But I'm - I'm not clear when that was.
MR GREGGERY: And when you did it. Alright. If we go over to the second page, we're
probably more interested in the substance of the advice. And if "DSS concerns" could
be - thank you. Again, to the extent that you may have become aware of this particular email
in 2017, it contained effectively a repeat of the issues about income smoothing that were
identified back when the proposal was first considered in 2014/2015?

MS HALBERT: That's right. Sorry, is this advice from Mr Mason in 2017 or -
MR GREGGERY: No.
MS HALBERT: No, it's -
MR GREGGERY: Mr Mason in 2015.
MS HALBERT: So this is the same kind of concerns that we had.
MR GREGGERY: It's the identical concern then which was brought front and centre, as it
were, at least in Ms McGuirk's mind, and potentially yours, in January 2017?
MS HALBERT: That's right.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. Now, could we please go to Exhibit 1393, DSS.5023.0002.2547_R. This
was an email from - or this is an email from you to Ms Wilson, 1 March 2017. The
attachment is the combined 2014 and 2017 advice. We will come to that shortly. But it was
what you were setting out as the proposed response to the Ombudsman regarding the legal
advice "due today". Do you see that?
MS HALBERT: They had asked a specific question of us, so we were answering that.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. And if we go over to page 2548, the specific question appears in the
middle of the page. If the email - thank you. And the request came from Ms Macleod, who is
noted in the footer as the Acting Senior Ombudsman, and the request relates to the advice
which appears in the Executive Minute briefing the Minister for Social Services dated 12
February 2015. This was a document of which the draft was considered by you in your final
email to Ms Golightly on Friday, 23 January 2015?
MS HALBERT: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And on page 10 of the document, it states that:
There may need to be a change of policy.
And that:
DSS also advised legislative change would also be needed to implement the initiative.
And what was asked by the Acting Senior Ombudsman was for a copy by 1 March 2017 of the
advice from DSS and any other notes, documents or emails that relate to this advice. And so
the proposed response that you drafted for consideration by Ms Wilson was set out in the
body of the email?
MS HALBERT: That's right.

MR GREGGERY: If we return, then, to the body of the email on page 2547. We will just deal
with these paragraphs sequentially, but perhaps if the first three paragraphs could be called
out. This is how your draft was, and I will just ask you to peruse that briefly. But in essence,
do you agree that you repeat in the first two paragraphs the position as it was
communicated to DHS in January 2015?
MS HALBERT: That's the case, yes.
MR GREGGERY: Yes. The last sentence of the second paragraph is that:
It is understood that DSS also indicated to DHS that legal changes would be necessary to
allow the measure as DSS understood it at that time to be implemented.
Again, that reinforces the DSS position at that time?
MS HALBERT: Yes.
MR GREGGERY: And the first sentence indicates that:
Following this, DHS took DSS concerns into account and made adjustments to the process.
Now, what adjustments to the process did you understand were made by DHS when you
make that sentence - when you read that sentence?
MS HALBERT: Well, from our research, so to speak -
MR GREGGERY: From your research, yes.
MS HALBERT: - at the time. So we understood that DSS had put several steps in place
between the availability of the ATO data and the eventual raising of a debt. So there
was - our understanding was that they had broken the nexus between the availability of the
ATO data and the raising of a debt through this - putting in several steps enabling the
customer to provide information, etcetera.
MR GREGGERY: Alright.
MS HALBERT: So that was our understanding of the difference. It wasn't just giving the
customer an opportunity; it had to be every opportunity and easy to do that - easy to
provide the information, etcetera. There was a whole range of different steps that they had
put in place - or explained to us that they had put in place that we felt had broken that
nexus.
COMMISSIONER: Just so I can understand that, when you say you thought they had broken
the nexus between the ATO data and the raising of the debt, you understood that the ATO
data would not be relied on to raise debts?

MS HALBERT: That's correct. It would be a source of information that might contribute to a
debt being raised, but it would not be the cause of the debt being raised. It's still a source of
information that's available, that can be used, but it's not to be used to raise a debt without
these other steps being in place.
COMMISSIONER: And what are the other steps?
MS HALBERT: So it's the opportunity for the customer to provide information, but - and this
is from my knowledge I gathered in 2017 rather than, you know, current knowledge as this
was being done. But when it was first implemented or at some point in the implementation,
there was no phone number on the letter for the customer to provide this information. The
Online Compliance initiative, I think, whatever that was called, system was very hard for
people to access in some ways. It was not easy for people to provide this alternate -
COMMISSIONER: I think you may be getting off point a bit.
MS HALBERT: Sorry. Sorry.
COMMISSIONER: I'm just trying to understand how do you break the nexus between the ATO
data -
MS HALBERT: Well, it was by the -
COMMISSIONER: Just hold on a moment. ATO data and the raising of the debt simply by
allowing the customer to give some information. Because clearly if the customer doesn't do
that, you're going to have the connection between the ATO data and the raising of the debt
still in existence, aren't you?
MS HALBERT: My understanding was that DHS was going to take every possible step to
enable the customer to interact with them. I think they did make changes, although they
were telling us about these changes. But for us, it seems that the debt would not be raised
unless the customer failed to engage - and this was after DHS had put in place steps to make
sure that vulnerable customers - people had changed address - all sorts - people who would
not have, you know, got the notification or wouldn't have had the opportunity. DHS had put
steps in place to make sure that they had every opportunity, they could contact DHS directly
rather than being forced into the online environment, etcetera. And only - and only if there
was no other information available - and this was the 2017 legal advice said this to us -
COMMISSIONER: Okay. Where did you get all this information?
MS HALBERT: This is information that DHS was providing us at this series of meetings, I
believe, that -
COMMISSIONER: In 2017 or -
MS HALBERT: In 2017.

COMMISSIONER: Okay. Thank you.
MR GREGGERY: You say:
By early 2015, DSS gained a better understanding of how the revised process would satisfy
the legislative requirements.
Now, the legislative requirements that you refer to there is the requirement to calculate
actual fortnightly income by - before a debt could be raised; correct?
MS HALBERT: That's my understanding, yes.
MR GREGGERY: Yes:
In particular, DSS understood that the intended implementation model provided recipients
with the opportunity to correct any information presented to them based on ATO data
matching, particularly smoothing of income data obtained from the ATO.
If we pause there, that opportunity to correct any information presented to them on ATO
data, particularly smoothing of income obtained from the ATO, was part of the proposed
draft of the Executive Minute on which you advised in the week of 19, 20 and 23 January
2015, wasn't it?
MS HALBERT: I would say that's correct, that there had to be a real opportunity. And I think
in the course of our investigation, we had come to the understanding that there had not
been real opportunities for customers to provide this information.
MR GREGGERY: But the legislation that you're considering here doesn't address the question
of opportunity; it addresses the question of proof of actual income -
MS HALBERT: Look I understand that -
MR GREGGERY: Please let me finish.
MS HALBERT: Sorry.
MR GREGGERY: The legislation you are considering here addresses the question of proof of a
debt by reference to actual income in any given fortnightly period; correct?
MS HALBERT: That's right.
MR GREGGERY: And that the position of DSS in 2015 was that averaged or apportioned or
smoothed income from PAYG data was not sufficient evidence of actual income in a
fortnightly period; correct?
MS HALBERT: That was our original position. And in light of the 2017 legal advice - more so

apportion income over fortnights unless there was no other information available, combined
with the fact that there was a likely overpayment. So it may have been incorrect assessment
on our part at the time, but that was the conclusion we came to once we had that legal
advice.
MR GREGGERY: Ms Halbert, that was your original position. What you represent in this
paragraph is that it changed in early 2015, not as a result of the 2017 legal advice.
MS HALBERT: So that's my - where my understanding is coming from.
MR GREGGERY: Yes.
MS HALBERT: In 2015, I believe that understanding came from the meeting between DHS
and DSS.
MR GREGGERY: But you weren't in the meeting?
MS HALBERT: No, I wasn't. And this information had been provided to me. Obviously I'm
talking about an historical event here. So the information has been given to me by the
people who had that information.
MR GREGGERY: What you described then in your answer is not contained in Mr Kimber's
summary to you in 2017, is it? This last resort concept and the application of income
smoothing?
MS HALBERT: No, I don't believe we had heard of the last resort -
MR GREGGERY: No.
MS HALBERT: - until 2017.
MR GREGGERY: So how could you possibly represent that by early 2015, DSS gained a better
understanding of how the revised process would satisfy legislative requirements?
MS HALBERT: My recollection is that we came - well, I received this information from others,
and that we came to that conclusion prior to the New Policy Proposal being finalised, that
DHS had changed their approach such that I - this was not first-hand knowledge on my part,
but they had changed their approach such that we felt it satisfied the legislative
requirements.
MR GREGGERY: But the legislative requirement is about proof of actual fortnightly income by
reference to averaged income. That's the point, isn't it? It doesn't matter when it happens; it
didn't satisfy legislative requirements.
MS HALBERT: The basic problem was always that if you are on a fortnightly income tested
